Nuclear retaliation against population centers is hard to justify on most ethical frameworks. Killing millions of civilians who had no say in their government's decision is, in itself, a grave wrong — the fact that someone else committed a grave wrong first doesn't transfer guilt to those civilians. But the counterargument is serious: the *credible threat* of retaliation is what prevents the first strike. A nation that visibly wouldn't retaliate invites attack. So the expected-value case for a retaliation policy can be strong even if any particular act of retaliation, considered alone, looks monstrous. This is the classic paradox of deterrence — it may be wrong to do what it is right to threaten.

That usually points toward counterforce targets (military, command, weapons infrastructure) over cities, and toward the minimum force that re-establishes credibility.
